title: You staged it, then changed it. Which version gets committed?
summary: The index holds a snapshot of the file as it was when you ran git add — not a live link to it. Watch a file exist in two versions at once, and commit the wrong one on purpose.
mental_model: `git add` photographs the file. Editing the file afterwards does not change the photograph. Until you take a new photograph, the commit will contain the old one.

steps.title: Make a change and stage it
steps.why: This is the version the index now holds. Note the number: 28.
steps.expect: M in the left column, and the staged diff shows 25 becoming 28.

steps.title: Change it again without staging
steps.why: Now the file exists in three versions: 25 in HEAD, 28 in the index, 31 on disk. Status shows M in *both* columns — the same file listed as staged and modified simultaneously.
steps.expect: MM alert.py — the double M is the whole lesson.

steps.title: Prove all three versions exist
steps.why: Three commands, three answers, one file. This is not a bug or a cache — it is the index doing exactly what it is for.

steps.title: Commit and get the version you did not expect
steps.why: The commit takes the index. 28 is committed; 31 stays on disk as an uncommitted change. Nothing warned you, because nothing is wrong.
steps.expect: The commit contains 28, and alert.py is still modified.

verify.label: the commit captured the staged version, not the disk version

steps.title: Do it properly
steps.why: Re-add the file to refresh the index, then amend. The rule is simple: `git add` again after every edit, or check `git diff --staged` before committing.

verify.label: the commit now has the final version
verify.hint: git add alert.py again, then git commit --amend --no-edit

steps.title: The check that makes this impossible
steps.why: `git diff` should be empty before you commit if you meant to commit everything. If it is not, something on disk is not going in. Two seconds, every time.
steps.expect: All three empty — nothing left behind.

verify.label: the committed version is the one you actually wanted
verify.hint: stage again after editing, then amend

verify.label: you fixed it by amending, not by adding a second commit

pitfalls: `MM` in status means the file is staged AND has newer unstaged edits. It is the most-missed signal in git.
`git commit -a` sidesteps this by restaging tracked files at commit time — which is convenient right up until it commits a debug line you meant to drop.
`git show :<path>` reads the index copy; `git show HEAD:<path>` reads the commit. Handy for proving what is about to happen.
GUI clients often auto-restage on commit, which hides this behaviour and then confuses people when they return to the CLI.
cheatsheet: photograph the file as it is right now
the index version of a file
index vs disk — must be empty if you staged everything
exactly what the next commit will contain
